title: Iran drags B.C. into dispute
article: The Chretien government held its fire Thursday after Iran launched a new volley in the diplomatic row over the death and burial of a Montreal photojournalist, accusing police in British Columbia of the "criminal" killing of an Iranian.
"We're not going to enter into a war of words here," Foreign Affairs spokesman Reynald Doiron said. "Based on what we know, we don't think the situations can compare."

Iran's charges stemmed from a July 14 incident in Port Moody during which Iranian Keyvan Tabesh, 18, was shot and killed by a police officer after he allegedly lunged at the plainclothes officer with a machete.

Tehran insisted on a rapid, transparent inquiry with wording that mirrored the Canadian government's demands for an investigation into the death in custody of Zahra Kazemi, 54, and the prosecution of those responsible. Tehran's new offensive began less than 24 hours after Prime Minister Jean Chretien announced he was pulling Canada's ambassador to Iran back to Ottawa.
The recall was to protest Kazemi's killing and her burial Wednesday in Iran, contrary to the wishes of her son, Stephan Hachemi, and the Canadian government.
The government is mulling further penalties against Iran, including economic sanctions and curbs on government-to-government contacts and travel.

Hachemi, who lives in Montreal, and the Canadian government had demanded the body be returned to Canada for autopsy and burial. The government now is exploring legal and religious options for having the body exhumed and brought to Canada.
Iran dismissed as unjustified Canada's decision to recall Ambassador Philip MacKinnon and began publicizing its complaints about the killing of Tabesh.

"Why have the Canadian police, who should safeguard the security of the people, committed this disgraceful crime which scared Iranian citizens living in Canada," Iranian state media quoted Foreign Ministry spokesman Hamid Reza Asefi as saying.
"Iran wants the Canadian government to give an explicit and transparent and satisfactory explanation about this criminal act and to hand over those responsible for this regrettable event to justice."
The family of Keyvan Tabesh was shocked to find itself in the eye of the political storm between Canadian and Iranian officials.
Family members said they had no idea the Iranian government was going to use the death of Tabesh to create a diplomatic incident with Canada.
"We were surprised," said Keyvan's sister, Rita, in an interview at the door of the family's home in Burnaby. "We never talk to the government."
"The problem is between Keyvan's family and the police," she said. "It is a social problem, not a political problem."

Rita said as soon as she learned that news of her brother's death was being mentioned by Iranian government officials, she phoned her husband, who is visiting relatives in Iran, to ask him to phone TV stations there and tell them to stop broadcasting the news.

Port Moody police spokesman Const. Brian Soles said Tabesh and another passenger, Amir Aghaei, got out of their car and rushed at police. Soles said Tabesh was carrying a machete so an officer fired five shots at him in what police say was self defence. Tabesh was killed and Aghaei was wounded.

Tabesh's family dispute that account. His mother, Forough Jabalameli, said that her son did not know it was a policeman who was confronting him because the officer was dressed in street clothes and driving a vehicle without police markings.
She also said the officer shot at her son's heart and foot without identifying himself or giving any warning shots.

Pari Saeedi, a spokeswoman with the Iranian-Canadian Community of Western Canada, said the Iranian government's comments are in direct retaliation for the Canadian government's demand for answers in Zahra Kazemi's death.
"This is bullying and the Canadian government should not buy it," said Saeedi, who left Iran in 1985.
Former Canadian ambassador to Tehran, Ken Taylor, said the Iranian government's call for transparency is "outrageous."

"It's total mischief and absolute nonsense to try and link the two cases together," said Taylor, who was Canada's ambassador to Iran during the 1979-80 hostage crisis and spirited American hostages out of Iran. "It weakens their own case by taking this step."
Port Moody Police Chief Paul Shrive said a homicide investigation is continuing into Tabesh's shooting.
